title: Life Is Like a Dream
author: Zhanran (annotator)
excerpt: (From the Dream-Wandering Collection: Reply to Commander Yang Yuanru)

inline.s: Dream-Wandering Collection
Reply to Commander Yang Yuanru

[The ancients said: “In a scene of heat and turmoil, it is hard to keep a cool eye.” Because the three realms are without peace, like a burning house, those who come and go within it are all cooked and scorched by it. If one would find a patch of cool ground amid the blazing flames, only one with a cool eye can obtain it. If one can, in the present instant, make a single thought cool, then of a sudden one sees the great earth all ice, and of itself takes no refuge in the world of body and mind. These men of great power from of old, who play amid the field of birth and death and can turn the dust of toil into Buddhist work and transform affliction into bodhi, rely solely on a lone cool eye and a single cool heart — what further spiritual power or wondrous function is there?]

The ancients said: “Though in a scene of heat and turmoil everything agitates the heart, it cannot withstand the gaze of a cool eye.” Because the three realms are without peace, like a burning house, those who come and go within it are all cooked and scorched by it. If one would find a patch of cool ground amid the raging flames, only one with a cool eye can accomplish it. If one can view the world with a cool eye and reach, in the present instant, a single thought that is cool, then of a sudden one sees the great earth covered all in ice (where is any heat or turmoil?) and of itself no longer takes refuge in the world of body and mind. The men of great power from of old, who play amid the field of birth and death and are able to turn the dust of toil into Buddhist work and transform affliction into bodhi — they rely wholly on a lone cool eye and a single cool heart. What further spiritual power or wondrous function is there?
[The three realms are without peace, like a burning house] The Lotus Sutra says:

“The triple world is nowhere peaceful, like a burning house, filled with every kind of suffering, most to be feared; constantly there are the troubles of birth, aging, sickness, and death, and fires such as these, blazing without cease.”

[He relies solely on a lone cool eye and a single cool heart] This means: when the mind is empty, the realm is of itself empty; all dharmas are beyond bondage and are originally free. The Diamond Sutra says:
“All forms whatsoever are false and vain.”
“Not seizing upon forms, abiding unmoved in the suchness of things.”

In these two scripture passages, “all forms whatsoever are false and vain” — this is the cool eye; “not seizing upon forms, abiding unmoved” — this is the cool heart. In the present sentence, “qú” means “he.”

[This statement is very easy to know, yet very hard to see. Even as the Buddha and the patriarchs take the single saying “all dharmas are like a dream” as the essential road to transcending the world, yet the wise and the foolish of the world can all alike say “life is like a dream.” Their words are similar, but their meaning is not the same. In truth they have never genuinely, with a single glance, seen through life as a dream. If one truly sees through it, then of itself one is able, at every juncture of glory and disgrace, advantage and harm, gain and loss, right and wrong, to flick one's sleeves and walk away — who then would dare to face the edge of his blade?]

This statement (“in a scene of heat and turmoil, it is hard to keep a cool eye”) is very easy to know, yet its true meaning is very hard to see. Even as the Buddha and the patriarchs take the single saying “all dharmas are like a dream” as the essential road to transcending the world, how few there are who see its true meaning! And the wise and the foolish of the world can alike say “life is like a dream.” Though the words are the same saying “life is like a dream,” the meaning in the words of the wise and of the foolish is entirely different. Although the foolish person says it with his mouth, in truth he has never genuinely, with a single glance, seen through life as a dream. If one truly sees through it, then of itself one is able, at every juncture of glory and disgrace, advantage and harm, gain and loss, right and wrong, to turn and walk away — who could then stand in his way? (The carp has slipped free of the golden hook and is gone; it shakes its head and swishes its tail and will not come again.)
[Flick one's sleeves (diào bì)] To swing one's arms and walk off — to leave without regard or attachment.

[In fact, within it there is nothing at all mysterious. As for the very first step, it is not without its method. When we live in the world, we must first take the affairs of the dream and set them before our eyes, observing them minutely. We must surely and truly see, until we reach the point where we cannot help but break into a great laugh. Having reached this point, of a sudden we feel that the ordinary saying “life is like a dream” carries a meaning entirely different. Taking that same place, with a single thought turn the present realm and set it within the dream to observe minutely. When you see the heavy, drowsy, upside-down state, of a sudden come to a fierce awakening. Then, looking back over your life, all the various realms you have passed through — if you seek them truly, you cannot obtain them at all. This very point where nothing can be obtained is the first pass by which the Buddhas and the patriarchs escape birth and death.]

In fact, within it there is nothing at all mysterious. As for taking the very first step, it is also not without a certain method. The method is this: when we live in the world, take first the affairs of this dream and set them before the eyes, observing them minutely. One must surely and truly look, until one reaches the point of not being able to help breaking into a great laugh. Having reached this point, of a sudden one feels that the ordinary saying “life is like a dream” carries a meaning entirely different. Taking this enlightenment of the great laugh, with a single thought turn toward the present realm and set it within the frame of “life is like a dream,” observing minutely. When you see the heavy, drowsy, upside-down state, of a sudden come to a fierce awakening. Then, looking back over your life, all the various realms you have ever passed through — even if you wished to take them as real, you cannot obtain them at all (you are altogether unable to). This very point where nothing can be obtained is the first pass by which the Buddhas and the patriarchs escape birth and death.
[Reach the point of not being able to help breaking into a great laugh] Master Hanshan's “Song of Waking the World” says:
Though in life a thousand wiles are spent, in death but empty hands remain.
Sorrow and joy, partings and reunions, clamor every day; long span or early death, poverty or rank, hurry all the while.
Do not contend in strength nor strive to win the day; a hundred years are but a theater stage.
In a moment the gong and drum are still, and who can tell the way back home

[Do not contend in strength nor strive to win the day] A person's life is like a white colt passing a crack — in the twinkling of an eye it is over. Its outcome is “not a single thing can be carried away; only karma follows along”: after death the hands are empty, yet the retribution of the evil karma created by contending and striving follows like a shadow into the lives to come. Therefore, do not contend for strength nor strive to win, and instead turn that energy and time to practice so as to end birth and death. [A hundred years are but a theater stage] A hundred years of life are entirely a play. [In a moment the gong and drum are still] In the space of an instant the gong and drum cease, and this play has come to an end (a lifetime is over). [Who can tell the way back home] One does not know how the play ends.
